findings.problem: parse_scores uses unwrap() on Result, which is a panic path. parse::<u32>() returns Result<u32, ParseIntError> for non-numeric input; unwrap() will panic on any malformed line. This violates the zero forbidden constructs rule (no unwrap in production code) and the panic-free standard. External input at boundaries must be validated and return typed errors.
findings.failure_mode: A single non-numeric line in the input causes an unconditional process panic. In a safety-critical or mission-critical context, this is an uncontrolled denial-of-service vector. No caller can recover or distinguish parse errors from other failures.
findings.fix: Change the return type to Result<Vec<u32>, ParseError> or similar, map each parse failure to a typed error, and propagate. Alternatively, filter/collect into an enum like Result<u32, ParseIntError> per-line and return Vec<Result<u32, ParseIntError>> if partial results are acceptable.

findings.problem: The function processes all lines from input with no upper bound. input.lines() iterates over every line without any limit, cap, or mathematical termination proof. Per Power of Ten Rule 2, every traversal of external input must have a static upper bound. Unbounded line iteration on untrusted input can cause resource exhaustion (memory, CPU, time).
findings.failure_mode: An attacker or misconfigured system can supply arbitrarily many lines, causing unbounded heap allocation via collect::<Vec<_>>, potentially OOM or CPU exhaustion. No timeout, cancellation token, or max-line-count guard exists.
findings.fix: Accept a max_lines parameter or return a Result with a resource-error type when the input exceeds a bound. Use iterator methods with take(max_lines) when the bound is known, or return an error when the count exceeds a declared threshold. Example: fn parse_scores(input: &str, max_lines: usize) -> Result<Vec<u32>, ResourceError>.

findings.problem: parse_scores accepts &str external input and returns Vec<u32>, silently panicking on any non-numeric line. The function does not validate, sanitize, or bound its input parameter. Power of Ten Rule 7 requires callees to check parameter validity and callers to check non-void returns. A fallible operation (parsing text to integer) must return a Result, never panic.
findings.failure_mode: Any input containing empty lines, whitespace-only lines, or non-digit characters triggers a panic. This is trivially triggerable with input like "\n" or "abc". The caller has zero recovery options.
findings.fix: Return Result<Vec<u32>, ParseError> (or a custom error enum). Validate each line: skip or reject empty/whitespace-only lines with a typed error. Replace unwrap() with ? propagation.

findings.problem: The function is 6 lines but has zero documented invariants. No maximum input size, no documented parse behavior on edge cases (empty input, empty lines, leading/trailing whitespace), no error taxonomy. The function signature gives no indication of whether it can fail, allocate, or what its complexity is.
findings.failure_mode: Callers cannot reason about when this function succeeds or fails. No #[must_use] on the return type (though it returns a concrete type, not a Result, so the caller cannot know to check). The function's contract is implicit and undocumented.
findings.fix: Add a module-level doc comment specifying: accepted input format, max input size, behavior on empty input, parse error handling strategy, and allocation behavior. Consider renaming to parse_scores_checked or changing the return type to Result to make failure explicit.

findings.problem: The function returns Vec<u32>, allocating a new heap buffer every call. No with_capacity hint, no preallocation strategy, and no alternative API (like a caller-owned buffer). For a parser function that may be called repeatedly (as implied by the crate name 'unbounded_parser'), this creates per-call allocation churn.
findings.failure_mode: Repeated calls generate GC pressure, allocator lock contention, and degraded tail latency. No allocation budget or budget documentation exists. In a performance-critical path this would violate the allocation discipline rules.
findings.fix: Provide an alternative API that accepts a caller-owned output buffer: fn parse_scores_into(input: &str, out: &mut Vec<u32>) -> Result<(), ParseError>. Or use with_capacity if input size can be estimated: Vec::with_capacity(input.lines().count()).

findings.problem: The crate is named 'unbounded_parser' suggesting a parsing/compilation role, but the implementation has no compiled IR, no prevalidation, no dense representation. If this parser is intended to parse a grammar or DSL that is then evaluated repeatedly at runtime, the current approach parses on every call rather than compiling to a prevalidated artifact.
findings.failure_mode: If the input format is a reusable grammar/DSL, parsing on every call is O(n) per invocation rather than O(1) lookup of compiled IR. This violates the prove-slow-execute-fast principle.
findings.fix: Separate parse-and-compile from runtime execution. Parse the grammar/spec once at acceptance time, compile to a dense IR (numeric IDs, precomputed lookup tables), then execute the dense IR at runtime. This crate should own the compile step; a separate runtime module should execute precompiled artifacts.

findings.problem: No rust-toolchain.toml present. No build profile specified (defaults to debug-level optimization for release). No workspace-level lint configuration. The crate has no pinned nightly, no feature allowlist, and no release profile.
findings.failure_mode: Without a pinned toolchain, builds may use different compiler versions with different optimization, warning, and safety behavior. No release profile means debug binary could ship with no optimization.
findings.fix: Add rust-toolchain.toml with a pinned nightly date and allowlisted features. Add a [profile.release] section with opt-level 3, lto = thin, codegen-units 1, strip = symbols.

residual_risk: This is a static-only review of a 6-line crate. The primary risk is an unbounded parser that panics on malformed input and allocates per call. The code compiles and the logic is trivial, but it violates multiple Holzman Rust rules: unwrap() in production-reachable code, no input bounds, no Result return type for a fallible operation, and no test coverage. The missing benchmark/profiler/evidence means no performance claims can be evaluated. If this parser is intended for safety-critical or high-throughput use, it requires: (1) Result-based error handling, (2) bounded input processing, (3) caller-owned buffer API variant, (4) tests covering empty input, malformed input, large input, and edge cases, and (5) benchmark evidence if performance claims are intended. The crate as-is is suitable only as a toy or prototype, not for mission-critical deployment.
